extracted.intended_audience: General readers and YouTube creators looking for information on YouTube policies, monetization, copyright and creator rewards
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes YouTube platform policies and standards relevant to monetization, content eligibility, copyright/Content ID, creator awards, and subscription/partner program eligibility. Useful for creators assessing whether videos or channels meet platform rules for ads, awards, and paid features.

rubrics_metrics.name: YouTube Partner Program (YPP) revenue split
rubrics_metrics.description: YouTube typically takes 45 percent of the advertising revenue from videos in the Partner Program, with 55 percent going to the uploader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the stated revenue-sharing arrangement for members of the Partner Program; context notes that the majority of advertising revenue goes to publishers and video producers who hold rights, and the company retains 45%.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertiser-friendly content restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: YouTube's policies restrict certain forms of content from being included in videos being monetized with advertising, including videos containing violence, strong language, sexual content, and "controversial or sensitive subjects and events, including subjects related to war, political conflicts, natural disasters and tragedies, even if graphic imagery is not shown" (unless the content is "usually newsworthy or comedic and the creator intends to inform or entertain").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also restricts monetization where user comments contain "inappropriate" content. The page records creator criticism (e.g., Philip DeFranco) that demonetization can feel like censorship and gives examples of problematic application (Boing Boing reported LGBT keywords resulted in demonetization). The policy has an appeals/notification process that YouTube said was improved to communicate violations and appeals better.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monetization eligibility requirements (subscription/watch-time/subscriber thresholds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligibility criteria for monetization and paid subscriptions have changed over time: in 2013 channels with at least a thousand subscribers could require a paid subscription; in April 2017 YouTube set an eligibility requirement of 10,000 lifetime views for a paid subscription; on January 16, 2018 the eligibility requirement for monetization changed to 4,000 hours of watch-time within the past 12 months and 1,000 subscribers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These thresholds are explicit gatekeeping rules for access to monetization/paid features. The policy changes were criticized for penalizing smaller channels; creators should check current thresholds as they have evolved.

rubrics_metrics.name: YouTube reserves right to monetize non-YPP videos
rubrics_metrics.description: As of November 2020 (US) and June 2021 (worldwide), YouTube reserves the right to monetize any video on the platform, even if their uploader is not a member of the YouTube Partner Program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This occurs on channels whose content is deemed "advertiser-friendly"; in such cases all revenue will go directly to Google without any share given to the uploader. Creators should be aware that platform-level monetization can override creator earnings.

rubrics_metrics.name: YouTube Creator Awards (Play Buttons) eligibility thresholds and materials
rubrics_metrics.description: YouTube Play Buttons are recognition trophies given to channels with subscriber milestones: at least 100,000; 1,000,000; 10,000,000; 50,000,000; and 100,000,000 subscribers, respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The trophies' materials are described (nickel-plated copper-nickel alloy, golden-plated brass, silver-plated metal, ruby, and red-tinted crystal glass). This is an explicit, publicly stated threshold-based award system for channel popularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright holder options and Content ID monetization/claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyright holders can locate and remove videos uploaded without permission or have them continue running for revenue; the majority of YouTube's advertising revenue goes to the publishers and video producers who hold the rights, with YouTube retaining 45%.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Nintendo enforcing copyright and claiming ad revenue for game screenshots, later offering the Nintendo Creators Program to share revenue (a program later ended). The page references Content ID and dispute/appeal processes and notes controversies about improper or broad claims; creators should expect copyright owners to be able to claim revenue or request removal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-roll advertisement prevalence and pricing (advertiser-side constraint)
rubrics_metrics.description: In 2013, a pre-roll advertisement on YouTube cost advertisers on average $7.60 per 1000 views; usually, no more than half of the eligible videos have a pre-roll advertisement due to a lack of interested advertisers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a market/practical constraint affecting whether an eligible video actually shows paid ads — eligibility alone does not guarantee pre-rolls will appear. Creators and analysts should note advertiser demand influences ad placement and revenue opportunities.
